Libnah (wilderness station)
LIB-nah
proper noun
Hebrew Libnah, “whiteness,” from laban, to be white, perhaps of white poplars or chalk; here a wilderness encampment between Rimmon-parez and Rissah, distinct from Libnah the walled town of Judah.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Between Rimmon-parez and Rissah, in the long roll of the wilderness marches, stands a single line: “they departed from Rimmonparez, and pitched in Libnah” (Num 33:20), and again, “they removed from Libnah, and pitched at Rissah” (Num 33:21). This Libnah is not the town of Judah that later sheltered priests, but a nameless camp in the middle of the wandering, a place remembered for nothing but that Israel tarried there and moved on. Yet the Holy Ghost thought it worth recording. The forty-two stations of Numbers thirty-three are a monument to a truth the pilgrim easily forgets: God keeps the account of every stage of the journey, not the mountaintops only but the dull middle, the camps where nothing seems to happen. Israel pitched and Israel removed at the word of the LORD, and each obscure remove was ordered by the pillar of cloud. So the Christian’s path is numbered station by station by a faithful hand; the years that leave no story are not lost years, for He that led them through the great and terrible wilderness led them by Libnah too. We are strangers and pilgrims here (1Pe 2:11), and the God who wrote down Libnah writes down our forgotten days. Take heart, wayfarer, in the unremarkable stretch: the middle of the march is watched as surely as the exodus and the entrance, and not one encampment falls outside His covenant care.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A wilderness encampment between Rimmon-parez and Rissah in Israel’s wandering (Num 33:20-21), distinct from Libnah the town of Judah; a witness to God’s faithful care over the nameless middle of the pilgrimage.

LIBNAH (wilderness station), a camp between Rimmon-parez and Rissah (Num 33:20).

Distinct from Libnah the walled town of Judah.

One of the forty-two recorded stages of Israel’s wandering.

A place remembered for nothing but that Israel pitched and removed.

A witness that God keeps account of every stage of the journey.

📖 Key Scripture

Num 33:20 — "And they departed from Rimmonparez, and pitched in Libnah."

Num 33:21 — "And they removed from Libnah, and pitched at Rissah."

Num 33:19 — "And they departed from Rithmah, and pitched at Rimmonparez."

1Pe 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Libnah the wilderness station recovers God’s faithful care over the obscure middle of the pilgrim’s way, the years that leave no story.

expand to see more

Libnah the wilderness station is one line in a long roll of marches, a camp remembered for nothing but that Israel pitched there and moved on. Yet the Holy Ghost recorded it, teaching that God keeps account of every stage of the pilgrimage, not the mountaintops only but the dull middle where nothing seems to happen.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A nameless encampment provokes no modern dispute; the only care is to distinguish it from Libnah the town of Judah. The principle to recover is the covenant faithfulness of God over the obscure years of the Christian’s way. The days that leave no story are not lost days, for the hand that led Israel through the great wilderness led them by Libnah too.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From laban, to be white; Libnah is “whiteness,” perhaps of chalk or white poplars.

expand to see more

Libnah — whiteness, from laban, to be white.

The same root names Laban and the white poplar (libneh).

A different Libnah was a fortified town of Judah (Josh 10:29).

This Libnah is a mere encampment in Numbers thirty-three.

Named among the forty-two stations of the wandering.

Usage

"Israel departed from Rimmon-parez and pitched in Libnah."

"This Libnah was a wilderness camp, not the town of Judah."

"God recorded even Libnah, the middle of the march."
